title: The Revival, the remembrance of death
hook: the final book prepares the soul for meeting its Lord
tomorrow: Dadi hands Amira a tiny, worn book. what's inside?

segments.voice: Yesterday, The Revival's two halves: patience in one hand, gratitude in the other. Today, the last book of the Revival, and a gentle heads-up: it's about death, told calmly.

Sunday afternoon, tea on the table, and a grandmother says, in the same voice she uses for grocery lists: when I die, keep it simple. A plain white cloth. Bury me quickly. Ask someone to read Ya-Sin. Her granddaughter goes cold. Why would anyone talk about her own funeral so calmly, like it's a trip she's packing for? Because, in a way, she is. Al-Ghazali ends the Revival, his whole enormous work, with a book on remembering death and what comes after. He put it last, where the whole work ends up.
screen: `TEA, AND A CALM REQUEST.` → `LIKE PACKING FOR A TRIP.` → `THE REVIVAL'S LAST BOOK.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an says it simply, in Pickthall's words: "Every soul will taste of death." And a hadith in at-Tirmidhi has the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, urging people to remember often the thing that cuts pleasures short. That sounds grim until you see what al-Ghazali does with it. He describes three people remembering death. The first is wrapped up in the world, and remembers death only with dislike, as the thief of everything they have. The second has turned back to God, and remembers death to get ready: to mend, to forgive, to finish what matters. The third knows God, and remembers death with something like longing, because it's the meeting with the One they love. There's a hadith in al-Bukhari that sits right underneath this: whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet them. So the remembrance of death isn't meant to frighten. It's meant to sort. Ask what you'd do with a day if you remembered it would end, and the trivial things fall off the table. The arguments that don't matter. The grudges. The phone at dinner. And here's what makes this a book for living: preparing to meet God, in al-Ghazali's telling, is mostly done on ordinary days, with ordinary people, long before the end.
screen: `EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.` · `THREE WAYS TO REMEMBER.` · `WHOEVER LOVES TO MEET GOD.` · `IT SORTS THE DAY.` · then, large: `PREPARING TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: Write one sentence by hand: what you hope your days were spent on. Then sit calmly with it, breathing slowly. If this feels too heavy today, set the pen down and simply breathe; and if you are ever in danger, call 988 in the US or your local emergency number.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE: WHAT MY DAYS WERE FOR.` · `SIT WITH IT, CALMLY.`

segments.voice: The Revival, one last time: its final book, on remembering death so the soul is ready to meet its Lord.
The line to keep: preparing to meet him, mostly on ordinary days. That closes al-Ghazali, eight days long.
